title: Bài sưu tầm 117 - Passage 1: The Dodo: Re-evaluating an Extinct Icon
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 117

The Dodo: Re-evaluating an Extinct Icon

Paragraph 1. For over three centuries following its rapid eradication, the dodo (Raphus cucullatus) has occupied an unfortunate niche in popular folklore as an emblem of evolutionary incompetence. Depicted in historical paintings and popular literature as an obese, clumsy, and dim-witted creature, the bird was widely assumed to have been doomed by its own physical ineptitude. However, twenty-first-century forensic paleontology, high-resolution CT scanning, and the reconstruction of ancient ecosystems have demolished this Victorian myth, revealing that the dodo was, in reality, a remarkably resilient organism superbly adapted to the demanding environment of its isolated island home.

Paragraph 2. Endemic exclusively to the volcanic island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean, the dodo evolved from an ancestral lineage of fruit-eating pigeons that colonized the archipelago roughly twenty-six million years ago. Finding a lush tropical habitat completely devoid of predatory land mammals, the birds underwent profound anatomical modifications over millions of years. With no terrestrial carnivores to escape, natural selection favoured a flightless, ground-dwelling lifestyle, allowing the dodo to conserve significant metabolic energy. It developed robust leg bones, flexible pelvic structures, and thick, shock-absorbing toe pads, transforming it into an agile terrestrial runner capable of navigating jagged volcanic terrain and dense rainforest undergrowth. The bird’s formidable, hooked beak—measuring up to twenty centimetres in length—was a formidable defensive instrument capable of delivering painful bites, as well as a powerful vice used to crack open hard forest nuts and fibrous palm seeds. Furthermore, cranial endocasts demonstrate that the dodo possessed a brain-to-body size ratio comparable to that of modern pigeons, along with an exceptionally enlarged olfactory bulb, providing it with a keen sense of smell to locate fallen fruit amid rotting vegetation.

Paragraph 3. The downfall of the dodo began abruptly in September 1598, when a Dutch naval fleet under Admiral Wybrand van Warwijck anchored off Mauritius to replenish provisions. Accustomed to an environment without terrestrial predators, the birds possessed an evolutionary characteristic termed island tameness; they lacked an instinctive fear of novel large animals. When human sailors approached, dodos made no attempt to flee, allowing sailors to walk directly into the groves and seize them with their bare hands. Despite the ease of capture, the Dutch held the bird's culinary qualities in low regard. Sailors nicknamed it the walghvogel ('disgusting bird') because its muscular meat was tough, oily, and stringy, requiring hours of boiling with cabbage to become marginally edible.

Paragraph 4. Historical records demonstrate that human hunting was not the primary catalyst for the species’ extinction. The existential catastrophe was the introduction of invasive exotic mammals that accompanied European ships. Settlers released herds of domestic pigs to forage freely across the island, alongside inadvertent introductions of black rats, hunting dogs, and crab-eating macaques. Because dodos had evolved without ground predators, hens laid only a single large egg per breeding cycle in simple nests constructed directly upon the forest ground. While adult dodos could fiercely defend themselves against humans, they were powerless against nocturnal nest raiders. Feral pigs rooted up the moist leaf litter, destroying fragile eggs, while rats and monkeys devoured defenseless hatchlings in their nests.

Paragraph 5. Within less than a century of human arrival, the dodo was gone. The last widely accepted sighting occurred in 1662 on an offshore islet, though mathematical modeling suggests the final individuals likely perished around 1681. Tragically, European naturalists realized the bird was extinct only long after the last specimen had vanished, leaving museums with virtually no intact specimens. The true physical nature of the living dodo remained an enigma until 1865, when a local schoolmaster named George Clark excavated thousands of fossilized dodo bones from the waterlogged peat deposits of the Mare aux Songes swamp. Modern digital biomechanical models derived from these pristine fossils confirm that living dodos were muscular, erect, and surprisingly slender birds, whose tragic demise was caused by an ecological invasion against which millions of years of evolution could not prepare them.

q8.text: Modern anatomical scans show that the dodo had a significantly smaller brain proportionally than living pigeons.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...possessed a brain-to-body size ratio comparable to that of modern pigeons..." → Kích thước não tương đương, không phải nhỏ hơn đáng kể.

q9.text: Dutch sailors primarily hunted dodos to supply commercial meat markets in Europe.

steps: Đoạn 3: Thủy thủ Hà Lan săn để bổ sung thực phẩm tại chỗ (replenish provisions), chê thịt dai không ngon, không hề săn để cung cấp cho thị trường thịt ở châu Âu.

q10.text: Overhunting by humans was the single most destructive cause of the dodo's extinction.

steps: Đoạn 4: "Historical records demonstrate that human hunting was not the primary catalyst for the species’ extinction. The existential catastrophe was the introduction of invasive exotic mammals..."

steps: Đoạn 4: "...hens laid only a single large egg per breeding cycle..."
